fix: No code change; in RECIPES_AND_TUNING.md §4.2 (line 787) label the 1,500 switch, the 0.1 share and patience 20/50 as conventions, and change 'On in every candidate fit' to 'in every Sobol candidate fit' to match tuning.py:953 and boosted_trees.py:74-78.
evidence: The app's methods text (boosted_trees.py:287-293) only states the rule; it never says early stopping 'chooses well' or that searching is 'better' below 1,500, which is the inventory's gloss. The 100-unit rationale is exact: n_plan counts the rarest class or events (tuning.effective_size and plan_size), so 1,500 x 2/3 (K = 3) x 1/10 = 100 stratified stopping units. Both referees' arithmetic objections assumed total rows, so I reject them. Referee B's small log-loss gap (about 0.003 at n >= 1,500) is about a compute/accuracy trade-off the app does not claim to optimize.

fix: Replace the fixed CR2_MAX_FEATURES = 200 cap (featurewise.py:61, used at :209-215) with a cost budget on rows x exposures, or fall back to CR1 on t(G-1) when G is large, and make the caption at featurewise.py:261 say t(G-1) when the Bell-McCaffrey df were skipped under BM_BUDGET (featurewise.py:291).
evidence: CR2 with Bell-McCaffrey df below the cap is correct and certified (test_3b against written-out matrices, plus the clubSandwich check), and the 'too narrow' direction holds for features that vary between units (referee B: 73.5% vs 95.6% coverage). I accept both referees that the refusal has no methods basis: timing _cr2_tests gave 1.3 ms per exposure at N=2,000, G=500 and 6.8 ms at N=10,000, G=2,000, so 5,000 exposures take about 7-34 s. A repeated-sample omics table loses every interval, p and q to a self-imposed limit. The text honestly says 'beyond what TurboTab computes' and offers a valid exit (one row per unit), so this is S2, not S1.

fix: Either raise the n_boot default for the percentile interval to 1,000 (decisions.py:293 and :622), or keep 200 and say beside MAX_BOOT (decisions.py:448) why the ms5 simulation shows it suffices here. Label MIN_BOOT_SHARE = 0.9 (stages/calibration.py:513) as a convention in the user text, and add a test of the 'fewer than 90% ... no interval is shown' branch.
evidence: Both referees' simulations and the ms5 known-truth test agree that the shown interval covers near nominal and that the drop-direction caveat (calibration.py:1083-1088) is right, so referee B's 'not established' changes nothing decisive. But a percentile interval at B = 200 contradicts the app's own sourced rule: decisions.py:448 cites Carpenter & Bithell 2000, and modeling.py:43 switches to a normal band at 200 for that reason. At B = 200 the 2.5% endpoint is the 5th order statistic, with a Monte Carlo SD of about 0.19 bootstrap SDs (about 10% of the half-width). The 90% floor has no source.

fix: Change 'only if' to 'if' in COMPLETE_CASE_ASSUMPTION (missing.py:75-77) and in row_loss_concern (missing.py:1763-1764). Add that logistic-regression odds ratios also stay unbiased when missingness depends on the outcome alone and not on the incomplete covariate (Bartlett, Harel & Carpenter 2015). Fix the nested 'Sound if ... only if' label at missing.py:139.
evidence: Both referees and the audit agree, and their simulations match theory: White & Carlin 2010 give only the sufficient direction, and complete-case logistic slopes are unbiased under outcome-only missingness, where only the intercept shifts. The stated regime includes logistic models. The behavior (complete cases offered second, MI recommended) is defensible; the necessity claim and its garbled rendering are the defect.

fix: No change required. Optionally, strengthen the n_repeat < 50 concern (stages/usual_intake.py:606-608) to say that with fewer than about 30 people with repeat recalls the tail percentiles are poorly estimated and the between-person variance can reach zero.
evidence: The claim rests on the identity Var(mean of k days) = σ_b² + σ_w²/k > σ_b². It is sourced (Tooze 2006, verified by the audit) and tested on a known-truth simulation, so the mean-of-days tails are too wide and ranking that view lower is right. My simulation (N = 500, true prevalence 0.20) confirms referee A that the variance-components estimate is noisier than the mean of days with 10 or fewer repeaters: RMSE 0.30 vs 0.08 with 2, and 13-23% degenerate fits. It wins clearly from about 30 repeaters (0.06 vs 0.08), so referee B's 'better even with 2' did not hold in my run. The app already warns below 50 repeaters, so this narrow regime does not make the claim wrong.

fix: In share_phrase (methods/usual_intake.py:1309-1311), recognize by name, as reads_as_iron does, the nutrients whose UL covers only supplemental or synthetic forms (magnesium from supplements and medicines, folic acid, niacin, supplemental alpha-tocopherol, preformed vitamin A), and say that for them only that form is compared with the UL. For the other nutrients, say that a foods-only share is a lower bound on the share above the UL.
evidence: I accept both referees and the audit: 'since the UL applies to total intake' is false for magnesium, folate, niacin, vitamin E and preformed vitamin A (IOM DRI UL definitions). A user whose recalls include supplements for these nutrients is told the share above the UL is a share at risk of excess, which overstates it; food magnesium alone often exceeds the 350 mg supplemental UL. The app prints this sentence unconditionally, never checks the nutrient or whether supplements were included, and has no test.

fix: No change required. Optionally, have the finding's detail (repairs.py:1124-1126) say to check the zero denominator at its source, since a 0 kcal day is itself implausible.
evidence: I accept referee B. An infinite cell is undefined and breaks every summary (audit MA-18: it crashed DuckDB's stddev), and blanking it is the minimal repair. fix: Add the August 2021-August 2023 phlebotomy weight (WTPH2YR) to WEIGHT_TIERS between examination and fasting (recognizers.py:1798-1805) or to NHANES_WEIGHT_PREFIX (recognizers.py:1714), so blood analytes name it. In least_common_denominator (recognizers.py:1985-1990), offer WTINT first when no analysis variable is recorded only on examined rows. Drop DBQ/DBD from _DIETARY_VARIABLE (recognizers.py:1817).
evidence: I accept referee A's decisive point, which the audit missed. With WTPH2YR in the table and total cholesterol recorded only on phlebotomy rows, I ran least_common_denominator: it returned WTMEC2YR with settled=True. WTPH2YR is read as a weight (read_design) but has no tier, and its prefix is unknown, so the values check never runs. The recommended weight therefore skips the phlebotomy nonresponse adjustment that CDC added for this cycle. The interview-only (MEC named instead of WTINT) and DBQ-as-dietary departures that the audit found only cost rows, not bias.

fix: In seal.measure's multiclass branch (seal.py:722-726), replace 1.96·√(0.25/k_rarest) with the class-averaged bound 1.96·√(Σ_c 0.25/k_c)/C, which came within about 1.0-1.4x of the simulated half-width, or else word the current figure as 'at most about'. Add a test of _auc_halfwidth against a hand-computed Hanley & McNeil value.
evidence: Both referees agree, and my simulation confirms it: the shown macro-F1 half-width is 2.5-3.5x the true one (for example ±0.127 vs ±0.052 for 3 classes, n = 300, and ±0.098 vs ±0.031 for 5 classes, n = 1,000), because macro-F1 averages C per-class F1s. The error is conservative, the figure is labeled approximate in PRECISION_NOTE, and the AUC half follows Hanley & McNeil exactly, so this is S2: it can push users toward larger holdouts.

fix: In teaching/content.py:935-939, say 'often not at random' (Fraser et al. 2009). Say that MI improves on complete cases, while coding blanks as zero is the field convention and works for rarely eaten foods. Badge the handling half DISPUTED, as NUTRITION_PACK §06 (lines 659-662) does.
evidence: The mechanism half holds: Fraser 2009, verified by the audit, finds excess true zeros, more of them in older subjects, which also refutes referee B's doubt on age. But the app makes the pack's 'often' categorical and badges the whole section SETTLED, though the pack marks the handling DISPUTED. It also never says what MI improves on. Referee A's simulation, consistent with the pack's own zero-coding note, shows zero-fill beats MI for intake when blanks are mostly 'never', so the drawer can steer users away from the better analysis for rare foods.
